messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai Chen's eyes still widened at the scent of whiskey on a colleague's breath, transporting him back to that fateful evening when a bomb ripped through the crowded pub where he had been celebrating a friend's birthday. As a prosecutor, Kai was no stranger to tragedy, but this event had shaken him to his core. The memories felt more real than any case file or courtroom drama – they lingered, refusing to be relegated to the past. In the aftermath of the attack, Kai found himself replaying the events leading up to the explosion, only to hit a wall of confusion and uncertainty. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have done something to prevent it, that his inaction had led to devastating consequences. This self-doubt seeped into every aspect of his life, including his work. As he prosecuted cases involving terrorism, he began to question whether anyone was truly who they seemed – even himself. As Kai delved deeper into the memories of that night, he started to notice a peculiar phenomenon: sounds reminiscent of the explosion would trigger an intense emotional response. The sudden crash of a door or the pop of a firework would send him spiraling back into the midst of chaos, his heart racing as if it were happening all over again. It was as though the memories had become intertwined with his senses, rendering him acutely sensitive to anything that might evoke them. Feeling exhausted and drained became an increasingly familiar state for Kai. Even after a full night's sleep, he would wake up feeling like he'd been running on empty – a tiredness that couldn't be shaken by mere rest or caffeine. This fatigue only exacerbated his feelings of guilt and inadequacy; if he couldn't even protect himself from the memories, how could he possibly safeguard others? The weight of these negative appraisals bore down upon him, making it difficult to articulate his experiences – including the traumatic event itself – in a coherent narrative. Kai's memories continued to feel like they were unfolding in real-time, rather than as relics of the past. This perpetual sense of being 'on edge' meant that any perceived threat could send him careening back into the midst of the explosion. It was this constant state of hypervigilance that made it so difficult for Kai to shake off the memories – they felt like a ticking time bomb, waiting to unleash their full fury at any moment. As Kai navigated his daily life, these triggers would frequently catch him off guard. A crowded courtroom or the smell of whiskey on a colleague's breath could be enough to send him spiraling back into the past, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios and self-recriminations. It was this never-ending cycle that finally brought Kai to seek help – he couldn't shake the feeling that if he didn't confront these demons head-on, they would consume him whole. For now, Kai clings to the hope that therapy might offer a way out of this labyrinthine nightmare. Though the memories still linger, he's desperate to learn how to quiet their hold on his life – to break free from the shackles of guilt and self-doubt that have defined him for far too long.
